opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the things that genuinely surprised me, actually. If you'd asked me ten years ago whether you could get this kind of intuitive physics, the way water sloshes in a glass, how light refracts through it, how a liquid splashes and settles, just from passively watching video, I think I would have said probably not. I would have guessed you'd need some kind of embodied experience, an agent actually acting in the world and feeling the consequences, the way a child learns by pouring things and knocking cups over.

What Veo suggests is that there's a lot more structure latent in observational data than we assumed. To predict the next frame convincingly, the model has to implicitly capture something about the underlying dynamics: viscosity, momentum, surface tension, how materials interact. It's not solving the Navier-Stokes equations explicitly, of course, but it's built some kind of internal approximation that's good enough to render behavior our own visual systems find plausible. And our visual systems are very unforgiving with liquids. We've watched water our whole lives, so we notice immediately when something's off.

I'd be careful, though, about saying it "understands" physics in the way a physicist does. It's more like the intuitive physics a good artist or an athlete has. It's a learned model of how things tend to look and behave, not a symbolic theory you can interrogate and extrapolate wildly from. You can still find edge cases where it breaks down, unusual situations that weren't well represented in the training data.

But for me, the deeper significance is what it means for world models. If you want AGI, a system that can plan and reason about the real world, it needs a good model of how the world works. Veo, and things like Genie, are early evidence that you can learn a lot of that from data. Liquids are a nice test case precisely because they're so hard to simulate by hand. In some sense, that's the whole thesis of my career: that you can learn the structure of the world rather than handcraft it. So it's quite satisfying, and a little mind-blowing, to see it working.

r001.rationale: The response says observational data contains latent structure and that predicting video requires capturing underlying material dynamics such as viscosity and momentum.

r002.rationale: It describes a learned internal approximation of physical behavior, but does not characterize that representation as low-dimensional.

r003.rationale: It says a system can learn structure about the world from data, but does not suggest that low-dimensional structure characterizes much of reality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the liquids thing is actually one of the more profound aspects of Veo, and it surprised a lot of us internally when we first saw it. Fluid dynamics is notoriously hard. If you wanted to simulate water pouring into a glass the traditional way, you'd be solving Navier-Stokes equations, doing expensive numerical computation, and even then getting the splashes and the surface tension right is very difficult. And here you have a system that was never given any of those equations. It just watched a lot of video.

So what's happening is the model is learning a kind of intuitive physics, the same way a child does. A two-year-old can't write down a single equation, but they know that if you tip the cup, the juice comes out, and it goes down, not up, and it spreads when it hits the table. They've built an internal model from observation. And I think Veo is doing something analogous. To predict the next frame well, it's been forced to internalize regularities about how matter behaves. Viscosity, how light refracts through a transparent medium, how a wave propagates and dissipates. You can't fake that convincingly across many frames unless something in the network has captured the underlying structure.

Now, I'd be careful here. It's not that the model has discovered physics in the way a scientist has. It doesn't have conservation of mass as an explicit principle it can reason about, and you can find failure modes where a liquid does something impossible. But I think there's a spectrum between pure pattern matching and genuine understanding, and these models are moving along it. What it reveals to me is that prediction is a remarkably powerful learning signal. If you ask a system to predict the world, and you make it good enough at that, it has to start building a world model. That's always been my view, going back to the early days, and video is interesting because the world is right there in the data, with all its causal structure, in a way that's quite different from text.

And the reason this matters beyond making nice videos is that this is a step towards agents that can act in the physical world. A robot needs intuitive physics. It needs to know what happens when it pushes a glass towards the edge of the table before it does it. So I see these video models as early prototypes of the kind of world models that will eventually let AI systems plan, imagine consequences, and operate safely in real environments. The liquids are just a very visible, very beautiful demonstration that the learning is deeper than it might first appear.

r001.rationale: The response says Veo learns from video and must internalize regularities and underlying structure governing how matter behaves.

r002.rationale: It describes an intuitive internal model of physics, but does not propose a low-dimensional representation of material behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not speculate that low-dimensional structure characterizes much of reality.

astra-6.text:
I think liquids are a fascinating test because they’re incredibly complex. You’ve got splashing, turbulence, reflections—all these things interacting. And we haven’t explicitly programmed the model with the equations of fluid dynamics. It’s learning from examples of what happens in the world.

So when it generates convincing liquid motion, that suggests it’s learned something about the regularities underlying physical behavior, beyond just what water looks like in a single frame. It has to capture how that appearance evolves over time.

The interesting question is how general that understanding is. Can it handle a situation very different from anything it’s seen? Does it consistently conserve the amount of liquid? A clip can look plausible without being physically correct. So I’d see this as evidence of an emerging model of physical behavior, but we need more controlled tests to understand how deep that goes.

r001.rationale: It says Veo learns from examples of what happens in the world and that convincing liquid motion suggests it has learned regularities underlying physical behavior.

r002.rationale: It discusses learned physical regularities but does not suggest they have a low-dimensional representation.

r003.rationale: It does not speculate that low-dimensional structure characterizes much of reality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think liquids are a fascinating test because they’re so complex. You’ve got splashing, turbulence, reflections—all these things interacting—and we have very strong intuitions about when they look wrong, even if we couldn’t write down the equations ourselves.

So when Veo produces convincing liquid behavior, that suggests it’s learned something about the underlying regularities of the physical world from visual examples. It hasn’t necessarily learned an explicit fluid simulator, but it may have developed representations that approximate aspects of those dynamics.

The important question is how far that understanding generalizes. Can it handle an unusual container, or a sequence of interactions it hasn’t seen before, and remain consistent over time? Looking realistic in a short clip is one thing. Reliably predicting what happens under new conditions is a much stronger test. I think that distinction is where a lot of the interesting research lies.

r001.rationale: It says Veo may learn underlying physical regularities from visual examples, which communicates inferring structure governing material behavior.

r002.rationale: It mentions representations that approximate aspects of fluid dynamics, but does not propose that this structure is low-dimensional.

r003.rationale: It discusses regularities in physical behavior but does not suggest that learnable low-dimensional structure characterizes much of reality.
